world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: (30) Basic H/L system: Also, contrastive rising (R), falling (F), and downstepped high (ꜜH) a. mɛ̀tì 'salt' mɛ̀tí 'town, settlement' b. yàlà 'net, hammock' yálà 'God' [...] (32) Lexical tone on all nouns, all adverbs/ideophones, most derivational/inflectional morphs a. Cf. the lexically toneless: all verbs/adjectives, some functional morphemes [...] (56) Phonologically: [...] b. Limba is tonal (both lexical and grammatical tone), like languages of 'Southern Atlantic', unlike languages in 'Northern Atlantic'
new_statements.citation: Rolle, Nicholas (in collaboration with Larry M. Hyman, Kondeh Mansaray & Daniel Ibrahim Kamara). 2024. A report on Limba, a Niger-Congo isolate of Sierra Leone. Colloquium handout, Institut für Asien- und Afrikawissenschaften, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, 9 January 2024.
new_statements.locator: §1.4 'Tone', items (30) and (32), p. 4; §4 'Big picture', item (56b), p. 9 (same wording in the ACAL 55 handout, Rolle, Hyman, Mansaray & Kamara 2024, §1.3 p. 3 and (46b) p. 7)
new_statements.rule_in_words: East Limba (Wara Wara dialect) is described as a tone language: a basic High/Low lexical contrast (plus rising, falling and downstepped H) carried by nouns, adverbs/ideophones and most affixes, with verb and adjective roots lexically toneless and receiving grammatical tone; the source says nothing about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning stress. Tonal notes: syllabic nasal prefixes are not lexically contrastive for tone (surface L) but can bear grammatical H; downstep after H vs rising elsewhere in complementary distribution; the West-Central Tonko dialect (not East Limba) has utterance-final H-lowering, which 'clearly does not apply in the northern dialects' (Hyman & Kamara 2025 fn.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone plus grammatical tone in phrases/clauses; citation forms and phrasal contexts both given. No stress domain stated because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Limba-Wara Wara dialect of Kabala/Yagala (Koinadugu), i.e. Glottolog 'Northern Limba' [nort2763] under East Limba [east2387]; Rolle's own CV links his Limba fieldwork to east2387. The handouts also cite parallel Limba-Tonko data (Hyman & Kamara), which is West-Central Limba [west2450]; the Hyman & Kamara 2025 papers saved here are Tonko only. Older work (Clarke 1922, Berry 1958, Mukarovsky 1962/63) is on the southern Biriwa/Safroko cluster, which Glottolog files partly under east2387 (Clarke, Berry) and partly under west2450 (Mukarovsky).

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Section 1.4 'Tone' (p.4): basic H/L system plus contrastive rising, falling and downstepped H; lexical tone on all nouns, adverbs/ideophones and most affixes, verbs/adjectives lexically toneless; p.9 'Limba is tonal (both lexical and grammatical tone)'. Data mostly Limba-Wara Wara (East Limba).
Used only to locate the Limba handouts, dictionary and the California Language Archive collection (doi:10.7297/X2G73CM2, Limba [lma], Kabala and Yagala 2022-2026).

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Tonal analysis of Tonko (West-Central Limba): most words all-L in citation form due to Final High Lowering triggered by L% boundary tone; fn.2 notes FHL 'clearly does not apply in the northern dialects' (Wara Wara paká 'uncooked rice'); states previous work on Biriwa-Safroko contains 'nothing tonal'.
